intro: Fourteen verses in three movements: a temple that hears prayer and settles sin (2 to 5), a God who steadies mountains and quiets seas (6 to 9), and a rainy season that ends in a harvest loud enough to be called singing (10 to 14). The grammar to watch is the object suffix. From verse 10 on, nearly every verb carries a feminine ending pointing back at the land: You watered her, You enrich her, You soften her, You bless her growth. The psalm also crosses the whole range of speech, opening on the word for silence in verse 2 and closing on the verb for they sing in verse 14.

stichs.en: For the leader. A psalm of David. A song.

verses.summary: Four labels stacked with no verb between them. The heading tells a performer what to do with the text before the text has said anything.

stichs.en: To You, silence is praise, God, in Zion;
and to You a vow is paid.

verses.summary: The psalm opens on a paradox and does not explain it. What is owed in Zion is silence, and the second clause makes the other half of worship a debt that gets settled rather than a feeling.

stichs.en: You who hear prayer,
to You all flesh comes.

verses.summary: God is addressed by a job rather than a name, and the reach of that job is stated at once: all flesh, with no restriction to Israel.

stichs.en: Accounts of wrongdoing have grown too strong for me;
our transgressions, You wipe them clean.

verses.summary: Sin arrives the moment the crowd does. The speaker admits he is outmatched by his own record, switches from I to we in the same breath, and hands the verb to God.

stichs.en: Happy the one You choose and bring near;
he will dwell in Your courts.
Let us be filled with the good of Your house, the holy place of Your temple.

verses.summary: The answer to sin is an invitation rather than a penalty. Being chosen here means being moved physically closer, and the reward named is an address.

stichs.en: With awesome deeds You answer us in righteousness, God of our rescue,
trust of all the ends of the earth and of the sea of distant places.

verses.summary: The scope jumps from the temple courts to the ends of the earth, and the verb answer keeps the whole thing anchored in prayer while the imagery turns cosmic.

stichs.en: Who sets the mountains firm with His strength,
girded with might.

verses.summary: Two participles and no finite verb. God is described by action in progress rather than by anything He did once and finished.

stichs.en: who quiets the roar of the seas,
the roar of their waves,
and the uproar of nations.

verses.summary: The list is the argument. Roaring sea, roaring waves and roaring nations are set down as three noises of one kind, so politics gets filed under weather.

stichs.en: The dwellers at the far ends are in awe of Your signs;
You make the gates of morning and evening ring out.

verses.summary: The ends of the earth from verse 6 come back as people, and the two ends of the day are added beside them. Fear at the edges, singing at the edges, joined by the phrase Your signs.

stichs.en: You have attended to the land and given it drink,
You enrich it greatly,
the channel of God is full of water,
You prepare their grain, for so You prepare the land.

verses.summary: The turn to rain, and the longest verse in the psalm. Every clause is water reaching soil, and the last one states the purpose without decoration: grain, prepared for people who did not make it.

stichs.en: Drench her furrows,
settle her ridges,
soften her with showers,
bless her growth.

verses.summary: Four short agricultural verbs at close range. Whether the first two are commands addressed to God or a continuation of the description is not decided by the grammar.

stichs.en: You have crowned the year of Your goodness,
and Your tracks drip richness.

verses.summary: A crown turns the growing season into an event with a shape instead of a stretch of weather, and the crowned figure is imagined driving through, leaving fat behind the wheels.

stichs.en: The pastures of the wilderness drip,
and the hills gird themselves with joy.

verses.summary: The dripping verb of verse 12 is repeated as the first word here, which stitches the two verses into one picture, and the wilderness is given pasture, which is the one thing a wilderness does not have.

stichs.en: The meadows are clothed with the flock,
and the valleys wrap themselves in grain;
they shout, they even sing.

verses.summary: The fields get dressed and then make noise. A psalm that opened by calling silence the right response ends with three verbs of sound coming from things that have no voice.

pardes.body: Three movements, each with its own setting. Verses 2 to 5 stand inside the temple: prayer is heard, sin is admitted, a person is chosen and brought near. Verses 6 to 9 walk out of the building to mountains, seas and the far ends of the earth, held to the first movement by one verb, You answer us. Verses 10 to 14 are a rainy season, from the first watering to a harvest that shouts. The frame is the clearest signal in the psalm: the second verse gives God silence, {{2.1}}, and the last word of the last verse is they sing, {{14.8}}. Nothing between those two points argues that the silence was wrong. The noise is what the silence turns into once it has passed through soil.

Three cruxes worth carrying. The first is {{2.1}}. Read from the root for being silent it gives silence is praise to You; read from the root for waiting it gives praise waits for You, and JPS 1917 took the second. The consonants do not settle it and both readings are in use, so the verse is genuinely disputed rather than merely ambiguous. The second is verse 11, where {{11.1}} and {{11.2}} are imperative in form. A reader can hear two commands aimed at God dropped into the middle of a description, or a description that keeps going in a clipped form; translations split, and JPS 1917 smoothed them into participles. The third is {{14.1}}, spelled alike as the plural of the word for a lamb and the plural of the word for a meadow, so the line is either meadows clothed with the flock or rams clothed as the flock's covering. JPS 1917 chose meadows.

Verse 4 does something easy to miss on a first reading. The speaker says the record of wrongs is too strong for me, singular, and in the next clause says our transgressions, plural. A long-standing way of reading takes the singular as a representative voice, one person carrying a community's account to the one place built to settle it, which is exactly what verses 2 to 5 describe. Verse 3 is read in the same expansive direction: all flesh comes, not all Israel, so the house in Zion is treated as the address of everyone who prays. The last movement is read as the rainy season in the land rather than as weather anywhere, which makes the psalm a thanksgiving said after a year that came out well, not a request for one.

The mystical reading takes the psalm as a description of descent. Silence at the top, {{2.1}}, because at that level anything said is already inaccurate; then a name, a house, courts, rain, grain, and finally noise in a field. Each stage is coarser than the one above it, and each one is the stage above made available to something that could not have received it directly. The channel of God in {{10.5}} is the working image for that, a measured flow rather than a flood, since what is above arrives only in the width of the pipe. On this reading the shouting of verse 14 is not a lesser thing than the silence of verse 2. It is the same content, arriving in the only form a valley can hold.
